sentences.text: Eosuchus minor is distinguished from the modern gharial by a narrow, smooth bar located on the parietal bone between the skull openings.
Both species share features such as a large air hole, an elongated nose, paired tooth sockets, and a W-shaped bump at the skull base.
However, E. minor differs from E. lerichei because its nose is wider and the prefrontal bones sit further forward than the tear duct bones.
The species name 'minor' reflects an estimated maximum length of 2 meters, which is significantly smaller than the modern gharial that can reach 5 meters.
A fossil oyster was found attached to the snout of an E. minor specimen, indicating it may have lived in shallow marine waters.
The genus Eosuchus was named in 1907 based on a fossil specimen discovered near the Belgian border in northern France.
This original name was first used to describe a single specimen found in northern France near the Belgian border, assigned to the species E. lerichei.
The species Eosuchus minor was originally discovered in 1870 by Othniel Charles Marsh but was initially classified under the genus Gavialis.
In 1986, the name Thecachampsoides was proposed for the species formerly known as Gavialis minor.
The name Eosuchus was officially applied to the specimens of Thecachampsoides minor in 2006.
A second species, E. minor, was named in 2006 based on material found in the United States that had previously been referred to various different crocodile genera.
Concave depressions on the skull bones of E. lerichei suggest it possessed salt glands and was capable of tolerating saltwater environments.
The strata containing both Eosuchus species are believed to have formed in a marginal marine depositional environment, likely reflecting the real habitats these animals inhabited.
Eosuchus belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea.
Eosuchus is classified within the class Reptilia.
The type species of the genus Eosuchus is E. lerichei.
Eosuchus is often classified as a 'thoracosaur,' a group of basal gavialoids that do not form a true evolutionary clade.
Eosuchus is distinct from other gavialoids because it retains a thin descending lamina next to the pterygoid bone.

It is currently accepted that a close relationship between Eosuchus and tomistomines is not the case, and that similarities between them may be superficial, representing primitive traits lost in more derived members like modern Gavialis.
Both Eosuchus and tomistomines possess a deeply concave deltopectoral crest, unlike the more triangular crests found in Gavialis.
The genus lived during the Thanetian to Ypresian stages, approximately 59.24 to 48.07 million years ago.
Fossils of Eosuchus have been found in France and in eastern North America, specifically in Maryland, Virginia, and New Jersey.
Recent studies suggest Eosuchus may not be a gavialoid or crocodylian, but rather a non-crocodylian eusuchian.
Recent reevaluations suggest E. lerichei is the more basal species and likely the ancestor of E. minor in Europe.
A recent re-evaluation of the holotype material of E. lerichei suggests it is a more basal species and would have been the ancestor of E. minor in Europe.
